nations.name: Scotland
nations.summary: Every short-term let needs a council licence before taking bookings or guests. Control areas in Edinburgh and Badenoch & Strathspey. Visitor levies arriving city by city.

rules.text: All short-term lets (secondary letting, home letting, home sharing) need a licence from the local council before taking bookings or receiving guests. Operating without a licence is a criminal offence (Edinburgh notes fines up to £2,500).

Two control areas: the whole City of Edinburgh (since 5 Sep 2022) and Badenoch & Strathspey ward, Highland (since 4 Mar 2024). In these areas, using a whole dwelling that isn't your main home as a short-term let very likely needs planning permission. Licence applications there may need planning permission granted or applied for (mandatory condition 13). Proposed control areas are not in force until the council publishes a designation notice, at least 28 days before the start date. Argyll and Bute is consulting (21 Sep to 15 Nov 2026) on a proposed control area covering Mull and Iona; Coll and Tiree; Islay, Jura and Colonsay; and Oban, Lorn and the Inner Isles. The council extended this by two weeks after correcting figures in its consultation materials (2 Oct 2026). Not in force. Highland Council has agreed to submit further proposed control areas to Scottish Ministers (council news, Sep 2026). Reported to cover Inverness City and a wider rural area; details UNVERIFIED because the council website was offline when we checked on 22 Oct 2026. Not in force.

Edinburgh: 5% of the accommodation cost, first 5 consecutive nights, stays from 24 Jul 2026, quarterly returns via visitorlevy.scot. First returns (stays 24 Jul to 30 Sep 2026) are due 1 to 30 Oct 2026, with payment by 13 Nov 2026. Glasgow: 5% from 25 Jan 2027, whole stay, liable on bookings made from 1 Apr 2026. Highland: consultation on £5 per room per night (opened 7 Sep 2026, closes 30 Nov 2026); council decision due 10 Dec 2026, then an 18-month lead-in. Aberdeen: 7% from 1 Apr 2027, whole stay, bookings made from 1 Oct 2026. Stirling: 3% from 14 Jun 2027, bookings made from 1 Jan 2027. West Dunbartonshire: 5% from 1 Jul 2027, bookings made from 1 Oct 2026. Dundee: consultation 31 Aug to 27 Nov 2026 on two options, £5 per room per night or 5% of the nightly room rate, both capped at 7 nights; earliest start 2028/29. Moray: consultation on whether to have a levy at all, to 31 Oct 2026 (no draft scheme yet). East Lothian: consulted on a draft 5% scheme (26 Jun to 18 Sep 2026); a council meeting on 27 Oct 2026 is asked to approve an independent review before any decision. Argyll and Bute: consultation on a flat rate per room per night closed 5 Oct 2026, no decision yet.
The UK-wide Furnished Holiday Let tax regime was abolished from April 2025. Income is now taxed as ordinary property income.

To pay non-domestic rates instead of council tax, a let must not be anyone's only or main home, must be available commercially for at least 140 nights in the financial year (1 Apr to 31 Mar), and must actually be let for at least 70 nights. Send evidence to the assessor by the later of 56 days after the year end (usually 26 May) or 56 days after their request. If you miss the deadline you pay council tax for that year. Lets to friends or family don't count. Small Business Bonus Scheme relief may apply.

nations.name: England
nations.summary: No national register yet (now expected March 2027). Use class C5 is still only a proposal. London has a 90-night cap. Business rates need 140 nights available and 70 nights let.

rules.text: A mandatory national registration scheme is coming under s.228 of the Levelling-up and Regeneration Act 2023. GOV.UK (updated 2 Oct 2026) now says it is expected to begin in March 2027. No regulations, portal or fee have been published yet.
The C5 short-term-let use class was consulted on in 2023 but is not law. Your local planning authority decides whether your letting is a material change of use. Councils can use Article 4 directions.
In Greater London, a whole home can be short-let for up to 90 nights per calendar year without planning permission. Going over that needs permission (Deregulation Act 2015, s.44).

To be rated as a business, the let must have been available for at least 140 nights and actually let for at least 70 nights in the last 12 months, and you must intend to make it available for 140 nights in the next 12. From 24 Jul 2026 there are easements for owners of 5+ lets on the same property, and for lets sharing land with another business.

On 10 Sep 2026 the government announced that mayors and Foundation Strategic Authority leaders will get the power to introduce an Overnight Visitor Levy, charged as a percentage of the accommodation cost (not a flat fee). Local leaders choose whether to use it and can offer exemptions (e.g. campsites). Accommodation providers would pay it to the authority. A bill will be introduced in due course; no levy applies yet.

The FHL regime was abolished from April 2025. From April 2027, property income (including holiday-let profits) gets its own income tax rates: 22% basic, 42% higher, 47% additional, with finance cost relief given at 22% (GOV.UK, published 26 Nov 2025).
Fire safety duties under the Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005, plus gas and electrical safety, an EPC where needed, and insurance (see GOV.UK guidance).

nations.name: Wales
nations.summary: Free registration with the Welsh Revenue Authority is mandatory by 31 March 2027. Councils can start a visitor levy (£1.30 per person per night); only Cardiff has so far. Licensing is legislated for, with a default start of March 2030. Business rates need 182 days let.

rules.text: From 1 Oct 2026, anyone taking bookings of 31 nights or less must register with the Welsh Revenue Authority by 31 Mar 2027. Registration is free and applies even where no levy exists.

£1.30 per person per night (75p for hostels, dorms and tent pitches). The earliest start is 1 Apr 2027. Cardiff starts 1 Apr 2027. Councils must give 12 months' notice. Isle of Anglesey decided on 24 Sep 2026 not to introduce a levy at present, and Conwy deferred any decision the same day. Gwynedd says it has not decided yet. GOV.WALES lists Cardiff as the only council charging the levy and no councils currently consulting.
A licensing scheme for self-contained self-catering lets has Royal Assent. Its legal default commencement is March 2030, with consultation on regulations first.

To be rated as a business, a let must have been available commercially for at least 252 nights and actually let for at least 182 nights in a 12-month period, and you must intend to make it available for 252 nights in the next 12 months. Stays over 28 nights don't count towards the 182, but those nights can count towards the 252 available nights if the property could have been booked for 28 nights or less (GOV.UK guidance, corrected 9 Oct 2026). From 1 Apr 2026 (Non-Domestic Rating (Amendment of Definition of Domestic Property) (Wales) Order 2026, WSI 2026/7) you can meet the 182 nights as an average over the previous 2 or 3 years, and up to 14 nights a year donated to a registered charity count. Otherwise council tax applies, and councils can charge a second-home premium of up to 300% of the standard council tax (cap raised from 100% for 2023-24 onwards by WSI 2022/370; each council decides whether to charge one and at what level, and statutory exceptions apply).

The Welsh Government is consulting (from 31 Jul 2026) on the criteria for classifying self-catering properties for local tax, including whether the 182-day letting threshold is right and 5 proposed exemptions (properties that are part of a wider business, large multi-unit properties, properties with a relevant planning restriction, properties within the curtilage of the owner's home, and properties on the owner's farm). It was due to close at 11:59pm on Fri 23 Oct 2026 but closed early at 5pm that day, so the Welsh Government has extended it to 11:59pm on Fri 30 Oct 2026. Email responses sent after 5pm on 23 Oct will still be counted. Nothing has changed yet, so the current rules still apply. We'll update this when the outcome is published.
Since Oct 2022 Wales has use classes C3 (main home), C5 (second home) and C6 (short-term let). Changes between them are permitted development unless an Article 4 direction applies.

nations.name: Northern Ireland
nations.summary: All tourist accommodation must hold a Tourism NI certificate. Inspections every 4 years. Fee £40 per unit (min £40, max £350).

rules.text: Under the Tourism (NI) Order 1992, all visitor accommodation needs a current Tourism NI certificate after an inspection. Certificates last 4 years. Star grading is voluntary.
Self-contained self-catering available commercially for 140 days or more a year is non-domestic (rateable).

The FHL regime was abolished UK-wide from April 2025. From April 2027, property income (including holiday-let profits) gets its own income tax rates: 22% basic, 42% higher, 47% additional, with finance cost relief given at 22% (GOV.UK, published 26 Nov 2025).

Belfast City Council is consulting (24 Aug to Mon 16 Nov 2026) on draft supplementary planning guidance for short-term lets, covering new-build and change of use of existing buildings (serviced apartments, apart-hotels, self-catering and holiday lets). The council says the draft is a material consideration in deciding planning applications. Elsewhere in NI, check with your council planning office.

councils.name: Isles of Scilly
councils.rule: 100% council tax premium on second homes (200% bill) since 1 Apr 2025, with national exceptions and a local staff accommodation exception. Holiday lets that qualify for business rates (140 nights available, 70 let) pay business rates instead. No licensing or local registration scheme. The Local Plan resists losing permanent homes to holiday lets.

changes.text: The Welsh Government has extended its consultation on the 182-day self-catering rule for local tax, and the 5 proposed exemptions, to 11:59pm on Fri 30 Oct 2026. It was due to close at 11:59pm on 23 Oct but the form closed early at 5pm. Email responses sent after 5pm on 23 Oct will still be counted. The current rules still apply.

Re-checked the Wales 182-day business rates rule against GOV.UK guidance and the Non-Domestic Rating (Amendment of Definition of Domestic Property) (Wales) Order 2026 (WSI 2026/7). Both confirm that from 1 April 2026 a holiday let that wasn't let for 182 nights in the last 12 months can still qualify if its average nights let over the previous 2 or 3 years is at least 182, and that up to 14 nights a year donated to a registered charity (for free use by its beneficiaries) count. The Wales page row is marked verified. The old GOV.WALES self-catering business rates page now returns 404, so we link to the GOV.UK guidance instead.

Added the published short-term let licence fees for Glasgow (from April 2026: secondary letting grant £310 for up to 4 guests or £494 for 5 or more), Dundee (£310 to £3,100 by guest capacity, same for every licence type) and Fife (£295 to £826 for a full licence by occupancy). Our licence fee finder now lists fees for all 32 Scottish councils.

Added council pages for Blaenau Gwent and Merthyr Tydfil, so all 22 Welsh councils now have a page. Merthyr Tydfil keeps its 100% second-home council tax premium for 2026/27 (full Council, 11 Feb 2026). Blaenau Gwent's own page says a 100% second-home premium starts from April 2026, but its 2026/27 return to the Welsh Government shows none, so we mark it unverified and suggest checking with the council. Neither has a visitor levy or an Article 4 direction on short lets; WRA registration still applies by 31 Mar 2027.

Added council pages for Caerphilly (100% second-home council tax premium since April 2025, still charged in 2026/27; long-term empty premium only after 2 years, up to 300% after 5) and Torfaen (no second-home premium: one of only two Welsh councils not charging one in 2026/27, though the council says it is considering premiums subject to consultation). Neither has a visitor levy or an Article 4 direction on short lets; WRA registration still applies by 31 Mar 2027.

Added council pages for Neath Port Talbot (100% second-home council tax premium since April 2025, plus a new 6-month premium exception from April 2026 for self-catering lets moved off business rates onto council tax) and Rhondda Cynon Taf (100% second-home premium since April 2024). Neither has a visitor levy or an Article 4 direction; WRA registration still applies by 31 Mar 2027.

Added council pages for Bridgend (second-home council tax premium rose to 200%, a triple bill, from April 2026, among the highest in Wales) and Newport (100% second-home premium since April 2025, which the council says can include holiday lets on council tax). Neither has a visitor levy or an Article 4 direction; WRA registration still applies by 31 Mar 2027.

Added council pages for Wrexham (50% second-home council tax premium, one of the lowest in Wales, unchanged since 2017) and Flintshire (100% second-home premium since April 2023, kept for 2026/27). Neither has a visitor levy or an Article 4 direction; WRA registration still applies by 31 Mar 2027.

Added council pages for Monmouthshire (100% second-home council tax premium, unchanged for 2026/27; a property moving from business rates to council tax is free of the premium for 12 months) and Vale of Glamorgan (100% second-home premium reaffirmed for 2026/27). Neither has a visitor levy or an Article 4 direction; WRA registration still applies by 31 Mar 2027.

Added council pages for North Lanarkshire (one licence fee for all types: £315 up to 4 guests, £472.50 for 5 or more; levy feasibility work under way, no consultation yet) and East Dunbartonshire (3-year fee £594 for a secondary let up to 10 guests, same to renew; council decided in 2026 not to introduce a visitor levy). North Lanarkshire has its own levy map row; East Dunbartonshire is shown as 'No levy: decided against'.

Added council pages for East Renfrewshire (licence fees by bedrooms, £972 to £1,293 for a new secondary let; no visitor levy proposed) and South Lanarkshire (2026/27 fees by guests, £381.43 to £953.58 for a secondary let, same fee to renew; visitor levy research under way, no formal consultation yet). East Renfrewshire added to the levy map's 'None proposed yet' group; South Lanarkshire has its own row.

Added council pages for Inverclyde (2026/27 licence fees from £508 for a secondary let; levy decision on hold while the council monitors the national rollout) and Renfrewshire (2026/27 fees by bedrooms, £927 to £1,274 for a secondary let; renewal fee not published; levy proposition being developed). Both added to the levy map's 'None proposed yet' group.

Added council pages for Midlothian (2026/27 licence fees from £541 for a secondary let; levy to be reassessed in 2026) and West Lothian (planning permission or a certificate of lawfulness needed with every licence application; two conflicting fee tables flagged). Both added to the levy map's 'None proposed yet' group.

Added council pages for Liverpool and Sefton (second homes pay double council tax since 1 April 2025; holiday lets exempt from selective landlord licensing; Sefton short-term holiday lets planning guidance; Liverpool City Region Overnight Visitor Levy not yet in force).

Added council pages for East Ayrshire (new secondary let licence from £250; visitor levy paused until Aug 2027) and Clackmannanshire (2026/27 fees from £514.30 for a secondary let; no levy proposed). East Ayrshire moved to the 'paused' row on the levy map.
Added council pages for East Suffolk and Somerset (100% second homes council tax premium since 1 April 2025; East Suffolk gives homes for sale up to 24 months' exception; no licensing scheme).
Added a council page for North Ayrshire, including Arran and Cumbrae (licence £300 or £480 for a new secondary let from 1 April 2026; no control area; visitor levy not yet decided).

Added a free "Is your licence renewal due?" checker for Scottish short-term let licences: estimates your expiry date and when to start your renewal, with renewal rules from the 1982 Act, Scottish Government guidance and council pages (Highland, Edinburgh, Argyll and Bute, Na h-Eileanan Siar, Angus).

Added council pages for South Ayrshire (visitor levy paused until August 2027 at the earliest; licensing policy and fees under review) and Angus (licence £349 to £588, renewals now up to 6 years; no control area), with licence fees and levy status.

Added 4 Scottish council pages: Falkirk (5% visitor levy consultation open to 25 Nov 2026), Orkney Islands, Shetland Islands and Na h-Eileanan Siar (Western Isles), with 2026/27 licence fees and levy status. The three island councils are not pursuing an overnight levy.

Added 8 council pages for holiday-let hotspots: North Norfolk, Dorset, South Hams, North Devon, Isle of Wight (100% second homes premium from 1 Apr 2025), Denbighshire (150%), Carmarthenshire (100%) and Swansea (100%), plus a free licence and registration checker.

Welsh Government consultation on how self-catering properties are classified for local tax (including the 182-day letting threshold and 5 proposed exemptions) closed. No response or decision published yet; current rules still apply.

GOV.UK Wales business rates guidance corrected: nights in stays over 28 nights don't count towards the 182 let nights, but can count towards the 252 available nights if the property could have been booked for 28 nights or less.
WRA registration guidance updated: register by 31 Mar 2027.
National STL register start pushed to 'expected March 2027'.
Argyll and Bute corrects figures in its control area consultation and extends it by two weeks, to 15 Nov 2026.
Duty to register visitor accommodation with the WRA starts.
Aberdeen (7%) and West Dunbartonshire (5%) visitor levies: bookings made from today are liable for stays from 1 Apr 2027 and 1 Jul 2027.
Business rates guidance adds rules for owners of 5+ lets and for mixed-use sites (effective 24 Jul 2026).
Isle of Anglesey decides not to introduce a visitor levy at present; Conwy defers any decision. Cardiff remains the only Welsh council charging the levy.
Argyll and Bute opens consultation (to 15 Nov 2026) on a proposed short-term let control area covering Mull and Iona; Coll and Tiree; Islay, Jura and Colonsay; and Oban, Lorn and the Inner Isles.
Government announces an Overnight Visitor Levy power for mayors and Foundation Strategic Authorities (percentage of room cost; needs legislation).
Highland opens 12-week visitor levy consultation (£5 per room per night proposed).
Moray opens a consultation on whether to introduce a visitor levy (to 31 Oct 2026).
Dundee opens a 12-week visitor levy consultation on two options: £5 per room per night or 5% of the room rate, both capped at 7 nights (to 27 Nov 2026).
Belfast City Council consults on draft planning guidance for short-term lets (to 16 Nov 2026).
Perth & Kinross opens 12-week consultation on a draft visitor levy.
Welsh Government opens consultation on the 182-day self-catering rates rule and 5 proposed exemptions (closes Fri 23 Oct 2026).
Edinburgh 5% visitor levy goes live.
Perth & Kinross agrees STL control area for Highland Perthshire and N. Eastern Perthshire (awaiting Ministers).
Gwynedd Article 4 direction ends after appeal refused.

Added council pages for Torridge (north Devon coast) and East Lindsey (Lincolnshire coast, including Skegness and Mablethorpe areas). Both charge a 100% second homes council tax premium, so 200% council tax, from 1 Apr 2025. Holiday lets valued for business rates instead do not pay it. Neither has a short-let licence or an Article 4 direction on holiday lets.

Added council pages for Cotswold (Gloucestershire) and East Devon (Devon). Both charge a 100% second homes council tax premium, so 200% council tax, from 1 Apr 2025. Holiday lets valued for business rates instead do not pay it. Neither has a short-let licence or an Article 4 direction on holiday lets.

Added council pages for Torbay (Torquay, Paignton and Brixham) and Brighton & Hove. Both charge a 100% second homes council tax premium, so 200% council tax, from 1 Apr 2025. Holiday lets valued for business rates instead do not pay it. Neither has a short-let licence or an Article 4 direction on holiday lets; Brighton & Hove says some short lets may need planning permission.

Added council pages for Bath and North East Somerset and New Forest (Hampshire). Both charge a 100% second homes council tax premium, so 200% council tax, from 1 Apr 2025, and still in 2026/27. Holiday lets valued for business rates instead do not pay it. Neither has a short-let licence or an Article 4 direction on holiday lets; the New Forest National Park's draft Local Plan proposes principal residence conditions on new homes.

Added council pages for West Devon (Tavistock and Okehampton) and Teignbridge (Newton Abbot, Teignmouth and Dawlish). Both charge a 100% second homes council tax premium, so 200% council tax, from 1 Apr 2025, and still in 2026/27. Holiday lets valued for business rates instead do not pay it. Neither has a short-let licence or an Article 4 direction on holiday lets; Teignbridge's new Local Plan requires new-build homes in five coastal parishes to be primary residences, and Dartmoor National Park conditions new holiday lets to holiday use only.

Added council pages for City of York and Derbyshire Dales (Matlock, Bakewell and Ashbourne). Both charge a 100% second homes council tax premium, so 200% council tax, from 1 Apr 2025. Holiday lets valued for business rates instead do not pay it. Neither has a short-let licence or an Article 4 direction on holiday lets; York has draft planning guidance on short-term holiday lets awaiting approval, and the York and North Yorkshire visitor levy report is now on both York and North Yorkshire pages.

Added council pages for Bournemouth, Christchurch and Poole (BCP) and the Isles of Scilly. Both charge a 100% second homes council tax premium, so 200% council tax, from 1 Apr 2025; the Isles of Scilly adds a local exception for staff accommodation. Holiday lets valued for business rates instead do not pay it. Neither has a short-let licence or an Article 4 direction on holiday lets. BCP Council agreed a short-term lets motion on 12 May 2026 (use existing powers, map lets, gather evidence for a possible future Article 4 direction); the Isles of Scilly Local Plan resists turning permanent homes into holiday lets. The visitor levy map now shows the BCP Accommodation BID charge as void (ballot declared void in Jan 2025).
